passages.original: Quod cum seueriore quam putabat uoce dixissem, subticuit aliquantum. et ego iam reliqueram coeptam et ad me redieram, ne frustra occupare praeoccupatum atque inepte uellem; tum ille: Egomet meo indicio quasi sorex, inquit, non dictum est commodius apud Terentium quam nunc dici a me de me potest; sed sane illud ultimum fortasse in contrarium uertetur; quod enim ait ille: hodie perii, ego forte hodie inueniar. nam si non contemnitis, quod superstitiosi solent, etiam de muribus augurari, si ego illum murem uel soricem, qui me tibi uigilantem detulit, strepitu meo commonui, si quid sapit, redire in cubile suum secumque conquiescere, cur non ego ipse isto strepitu uocis tuae commonear philosophari potius quam cantare?
passages.english: When I had said this in a sterner voice than he expected, he fell silent for a while. I too had already dropped the line of thought I had begun and had returned to myself, so as not to wish, pointlessly and foolishly, to occupy one who was already occupied. Then he said: "'I myself, by my own giveaway, like a shrew-mouse': nothing was said more aptly in Terence than can now be said by me about myself. But perhaps that last part will be turned to the contrary; for what he says, 'today I am lost,' I perhaps today may be found. For if you do not despise what superstitious people are accustomed to do, taking auguries even from mice, then if I, by my noise, warned that mouse or shrew-mouse which reported to you that I was awake to go back, if it has any sense, into its bed and rest quietly by itself, why should I not myself be warned by this noise of your voice to philosophize rather than sing?"
passages.notes: The quotation is from Terence, Eunuchus 1024: 'egomet meo indicio miser quasi sorex hodie perii' ('I, wretch, like a shrew-mouse, have perished today by my own giveaway'). There is a wordplay on perii ('I am lost/perished') versus inueniar ('I may be found'). The construction of the long conditional is somewhat compressed; the sense is that the mouse whose noise betrayed Licentius' wakefulness was itself warned by his noise to go back to rest.

passages.original: nihil autem horum facere poterat, si multitudo rerum sine quodam defixo termino infinito patere uideretur. ergo utilitas numerandi magna necessitate animaduersa est. quibus duobus repertis nata est illa librariorum et calculonum professio uelut quaedam grammaticae infantia, quam Uarro litterationem uocat; Graece autem quomodo appelletur, non satis in praesentia recolo.
passages.english: But it could do none of these things if the multitude of things seemed to stretch out without limit, with no fixed boundary. So the usefulness of counting was recognized, out of great necessity. When these two [things] had been discovered, there arose that profession of copyists and calculators, as a kind of infancy of grammar, which Varro calls *litteratio* [elementary instruction in letters]; what it is called in Greek I do not quite recall at present.
passages.notes: "calculonum" is read as "calculatorum" (calculators, reckoning-teachers). The form may be a variant or a corruption. "These two" refers to letters and numbers.
